title: How Airbnb Makes Money
fullText: Sometime in the next few weeks, depending on which country your host lives in, the service fee is going to vanish off your Airbnb checkout page. You will search a city, find somewhere with a nice kitchen, tap through to pay, and the row that has irritated you on every booking you have ever made will simply not be there. Airbnb has not decided to charge you less. It will actually collect a little more from the same booking than it does today. What it has done is move the fee somewhere you cannot see it and it has published the exact date it intends to finish the job. This is how Airbnb makes money. To follow any of it, you have to know how the money currently splits, which is something most people booking a holiday have never had a reason to work out. Imagine the nightly rate times the nights comes to $1,000 and that,000 is the number your host chose. Airbnb then reaches into the transaction twice. It takes 3% off the host who ends up with 970 and it adds roughly 14% onto you. So the card gets charged 1,140. You have seen that second number. your whole booking life sitting in its own row under the subtotal. And it is comfortably the most complained about line item in modern travel. $1,140 leaving your account for a house whose owner receives 970 of it. The remaining 170 goes to a company that owns nothing you are about to sleep in, cleans nothing, and will not be handing you any keys. On the 7th of July this year, Airbnb confirmed when that arrangement ends. Hosts outside the EU move over on the 15th of September. Host inside of it on the 13th of October and from then there is a single fee of 15 12% which the host pays in full. Your line disappears. I would hold off deciding what you think about that because the fee itself turns out to be the boring half. What happens to the advertised price afterwards is the interesting half. Plenty of you have hosted and I will come to you in a second. For everyone who has only ever been the guest, let me make a bet about you. You have never once checked what your host actually received. You looked at the total. You made a small noise and booked it anyway. And then you complained about the fee somewhere between the airport and the front door without ever establishing where the money went. Go ahead and prove me wrong. If you know what your host was paid on the last booking, put both figures in the comments, the number you paid and the number they got. And if you host, post your payout next to the guest total because hosts are the only people in this entire arrangement who can see both halves at once. And the gap does something to guess every time somebody puts it up. Like this video if you have ever argued with someone about an Airbnb fee. Subscribe if you would like to know why it exists. Back to the disappearing line, then. A host currently clearing $970 on that $1,000 booking wakes up in September to a problem because Airbnb now takes $15.5% of the entire thing rather than three. Leave the listing untouched and the payout drops to $845 for the identical house. The identical night and the identical guest, which is about 13% less money for no reason the host can explain to themselves. Nobody accepts that. So hosts will do the only thing that the situation allows, which is push the listed price up until the payout climbs back to where it was. Getting $970 out the other side of a 15.5% cut means advertising the place at $1,148. Have a look at what has happened to your screen in the meantime. Before you were staring at a $1,000 place with a $140 of fees bolted onto it, and your annoyance had a target. Afterwards, you're looking at a place that cost $1,148 to stay in with no fees anywhere on the page, and the annoyance has nothing to attach itself to. You are paying $8 more than you were. Airbnb is collecting 178 rather than 170. Your host is precisely where they started and the single most resented number in the business has been folded into the price of the room where it now reads as something the host decided rather than something Airbnb took. Nobody reduced a fee. A fee was dissolved into a figure you had already agreed to look at. There is a decent argument on the other side of this and it deserves saying properly. Guests really do prefer one honest number. Hotels spent two decades being sued over resort fees and drip pricing. And regulators in several countries now insist on a total price upfront. Airbnb can stand there with a straight face and say it is finally shown you what the stay costs and it would be telling the truth. The truth just happens to arrive on the same morning that the thing everybody was angry about becomes impossible to see. So much for the fee. The scale of it is a separate shock. $91.3 billion of bookings went through Airbnb last year, which is what guests collectively paid for 533 million nights and experiences. Out of that river, the company kept 12.24 billion, and that figure is its entire revenue. Every remaining dollar belonged to somebody with a spare bedroom or a second flat, 13.4%. Airbnb handles $91 billion of other people's transactions and retains roughly $1 in every 7 and a half, which sounds almost restrained until you look at what earning it costs. There are more than 8 million active listings on the platform spread across more than 220 countries, and Airbnb owns exactly none of them. No buildings, no mortgages, no housekeepers on payroll, no empty rooms bleeding money through February. A hotel group operating 8 million rooms would represent the largest construction project in the history of our species. An Airbnb covers the same ground with a balance sheet that has no property on it whatsoever, which explains the profits once you see it written down. 12.24 24 billion of revenue produced 2.51 billion of net income last year. A 20.5% net margin achieved in a year when net income actually fell 5% because the company spent more on staff and advertising. Free cash flow came in at $4.6 billion, meaning 38 cents of every revenue dollar landed as cash the business could do whatever it liked with. Set that beside the industry it grew out of. A hotel chain that genuinely owns its rooms considers a high singledigit net margin a decent year because it is paying for roofs and laundry and refurbishment cycles and the nights nobody books. Airbnb pays for a website, a payment system, an insurance program, and an enormous amount of advertising, then keeps a fifth of everything that moves. People tend to draw the wrong conclusion from that and getting it wrong makes the rest of the company unreadable. The lazy version says Airbnb is a website connecting two strangers. So obviously it is profitable since it does nothing but accommodation was not invented in 2007 and there was never anything stopping you renting a stranger's flat in Lisbon. What you could not do was find the flat, believe the photographs of it, wire money 4,000 miles to somebody whose surname you did not know, feel confident anybody would answer if the place turned out to be a building site, or feel confident the stranger would not simply keep your deposit and stop replying. Selling somebody the willingness to do all of that is the actual product. The room was always there. Every corner of the business follows logically once you accept it. Reviews exist so the flat becomes believable. Photograph verification exists so the reviews become believable. Payments run through Airbnb so neither party can rob the other. Host protection exists so a homeowner will hand keys to a stranger from the internet. The company manufactured a quantity of trust that did not previously exist between two random people and 15 and a half% is the price it charges for supplying it. Once you see the business that way, a project everyone treats as a vanity exercise starts making sense. Airbnb keeps pushing experiences, meaning cooking classes and walking tours are some bloke taking you diving. And every time it does, a chunk of the internet rolls its eyes and tells the company to stick to houses. Look at what is genuinely being sold, though, and an experience is the purest version of it available. Because there is no room in the transaction at all, a stranger in a city you do not know takes your money and promises to turn up. Strip the accommodation out. That is what is left. Notice, too, that the number the company reports is not nights. It is nights and experiences together, 533 million of them. Airbnb has no ambition to become a tour operator. It is testing whether trusts built for houses will transfer to anything else it fancy selling. Because if the answer is yes, the market it is addressing stops being bedrooms and becomes every transaction that has ever happened between a traveler and a stranger. The business does not carry one enormous cost and forgetting it is how people end up describing this as a website that prints money. Roughly 18% of revenue goes on sales and marketing which on 12.24 billion means comfortably over $2 billion a year. And it is the main reason that net margin reads 20% instead of 40. Odd when you consider what Airbnb has become linguistically. The name is a verb. People say they will Airbnb it in the way they say they will Google something. And a brand absorbed into everyday speech ought not to need to buy its own customers, it buys them anyway because the instant somebody types a city name into a search engine instead of opening the app. Airbnb is back in a bidding war with booking, Expedia, and every hotel chain alive, paying for a click on a traveler who had already decided to travel. Fame does not exempt a company from paying a toll on the road to its own front door. And that 2 billion is not a growth expense waiting to be switched off one day. It is closer to rent, which brings us to where all this money physically sits, which almost nobody thinks about. You book in March for a trip in July and you pay Airbnb in March. Your host does not see a penny in March. Hosts are paid roughly 24 hours after the guest checks in, which in this example means July. For 4 months, that money belongs to neither of you and it is sitting with Airbnb. Multiply the gap by 533 million bookings and it stops being a technicality about payment processing. In June, at the end of the booking season, the figure was 11.1 billion. There is another 1.8 billion of fees collected against days that have not happened yet. 11 billion of other people's cash sitting on the balance sheet. Through a period when interest rates were the highest they have been in a generation, Airbnb did not lend it out or do anything exotic with it. The money sits in cash and short-term deposits, earns interest in the ordinary way, and the interest belongs to Airbnb rather than to the people whose money it is. Being the party in the middle is a structural entirely legal advantage. And the bigger the summer, the bigger the pile. Anyone who watched the ski resorts video will recognize the instrument because it is the same one aimed at a different industry. Money collected months ahead of the service. banked earning for the company throughout the weight. The difference worth noting is that a ski resort holds your money against costs it will genuinely incur. Whereas Airbnb is holding somebody's else's money in transit and taking the yield as it passes through. Hosts deserve a fair hearing here because there is a version of this where Airbnb is squeezing them and a version where it is not and both need saying. 15 12% sound savage until you price the alternative. A hotel selling rooms through booking or Expedia routinely pays commission in the same range or worse on a room. It also had to build and maintain. Airbnb's cut sits roughly where the industry sits and it is broadly the going rate for demand. What has changed is not the size of the number but what the number attaches to. Under the new structure, the 15.5% comes off the whole booking value rather than the nightly rate alone, which means the nightly rate, the cleaning fee, the pet fee, and anything else a host adds on. Airbnb now takes a cut of your cleaning fee. Worth pausing on the cleaning fee generally given it is the second most resented number in this business and is widely misunderstood. Guests assume the money reaches a cleaner, and some of it does, but it functions as a lever rather than a cost line. A host who lists a low nightly rate against a fat cleaning fee, looks cheap in the search results, where nightly price is what you sort and filter by, and then recovers the difference at checkout once you have already fallen for the photographs. Airlines have been running the same play for years. Cheap seat, expensive bag. The company has spent years trying to kill that behavior and its motive is entirely self-interested rather than noble because a listing that looks cheap and checks out expensive corrods the one thing Airbnb genuinely sells. Displaying total prices upfront was aimed squarely at the practice. Charging 15 12% on the cleaning fee is aimed at it too and happens to be extremely lucrative which is about the most Airbnb solution to a single problem imaginable. There is a larger shift underneath all of this though and the brand still does not say it out loud. The founding story involves a spare room and two men with an air mattress and that story appears in every profile of the company ever written. For years, the marketing leaned on somebody covering their rent by letting out the box room. Whatever that was, it is not the business now. The listings that matter commercially are whole homes run by people who own more than one of them, priced by software, cleaned by contractors, and managed by firms that exist purely to operate other people's short-term rentals. A great deal of Airbnb supply is not somebody sharing their home at all. It is a small hospitality business that concluded a flat makes a better hotel room than the hotel room does. Airbnb did not simply build a marketplace for spare capacity. It brought an entirely new category of landlord into being and those landlords then started buying property specifically to feed it, which is where the genuine risk to this company lives. and it has nothing to do with competitors. A rival problem would show up in the take rate and there is no sign of one. $91 billion still came through the door last year, up 12%. The risk is that the thing being sold becomes illegal. New York is the clearest example anyone has. Local law 18 requires hosts to register, requires the hosts to be physically present throughout the stay, and caps the booking at two guests. Read as a rule book, it sounds like paperwork. Read as a business condition, it is an extinction event for the entire home listing, which is the profitable half of the market because you cannot run an investment flat as a hotel while asleep in the spare room. Barcelona took a blunderter route, announcing it will not renew roughly 10,000 short-term rental licenses it has issued. So, when the last of them expire in 2028, the legal tourist apartment in that city ceases to exist. New York is worth staying with for a moment because it has now run long enough that we know what happens. The law took effect in September 2023, and short-term listings fell off a cliff, dropping from over 22,000 to somewhere around 4,000. More than 8 in 10 gone inside a year. Whatever anybody thinks of the policy, it worked as a demolition. What replaced them is the argument. Hotel rates in the city hit a record with the 12-month average nightly rate reaching $320 and the September peak averaging $524 a night, which is roughly what happens when you remove 20,000 rooms from a market and leave demand where it was. The housing question is genuinely contested and needs handling care. The law was sold as a way of returning flats to residents and pulling rents down. Manhattan rents have risen since it passed and vacancy has barely shifted. The loudest publisher of that finding, however, is Airbnb's own impact team, who have an obvious interest in the law appearing to fail. So, treat the figures as real and the framing as motivated. Housing economists will also point out that 20,000 units in a city of 8 and a half million people was never going to move rents dramatically in either direction. What nobody disputes is who absorbed the damage and it was not Airbnb. New York revenue was a modest slice of a global book and the share price barely noticed. The people who lost were hosts who built something on top of a rule that then changed. Here is where owning nothing stops being purely an advantage. Because Airbnb holds no property. No city can shut it down. There is no building to padlock and no license to revoke. For exactly the same reason, it cannot defend its supply either. A hotel group facing a hostile city council, as a physical asset, a license, a lobbying department, and decades of local relationships. Airbnb has 8 million individual people. it has mostly never met. Each personally liable for their own local law, any of whom can be legislated out of business without the company losing a scent of property. Carrying none of the downside of ownership also means owning none of the ground you are standing on. Pull the whole thing together and it looks like this. Airbnb is best understood as a payments and trust company that happens to sell nights rather than a hospitality business. It moves 91.3 billion of other people's money in a year and then keeps 13% of it somewhere between 7 and 11 billion of that company is sitting with the company at any given moment parked between your payment and your host's payout owning interest that belongs to Airbnb. It owns none of the 8 million properties involved, which is how the whole arrangement converts into a 20.5% net margin and $4.6 billion of free cash flow that no hotel chain on Earth could match. And in September, it removes the most visible evidence of all this from your screen. No fee is being cut. The fee moves onto the host. The host raises the price to survive it. And the identical money arrives at Airbnb through a number that now looks like the cost of the room. The honest reading is not that you are being robbed. 13.4% to locate a stranger's home in a city you have never visited. Pay for it without fear and of somebody to ring when the key box is empty. It is a defensible price and plenty of people would hand it over cheerfully if it were presented plainly. What is happening is more subtle and more interesting than a ripoff. A company that spent a decade being shouted at about one number has worked out that the cheapest way to end an argument is not to lower the number. It is to stop showing it to you. Next time you book somewhere, do the thing nobody does and work backwards from the total to what your host is receiving. If the listing says $1,148 and there is no invisible fee anywhere on the page, the fee has not gone. $178 of it is in there hiding inside the price of the room. If that has changed how the checkout page looks to you, leave a like and subscribe if you want the next one because there is always a number somewhere that somebody has worked very hard to stop you from noticing. The ski resorts video is the closest relative to this one. Another business built on taking your money months before it owes you anything. And the full money and business playlist can be seen on screen now. Bye-bye. I am waiting.
fullTextVi: Đôi khi trong vài tuần tới, tùy thuộc vào quốc gia mà chủ nhà của bạn sinh sống, phí dịch vụ sẽ biến mất khỏi trang thanh toán Airbnb của bạn. Bạn sẽ tìm kiếm một thành phố, tìm nơi nào đó có một căn bếp đẹp, nhấn vào trả tiền và sự ồn ào khiến bạn khó chịu trong mỗi lần đặt phòng được thực hiện sẽ đơn giản là không có ở đó. Airbnb vẫn chưa quyết định tính phí cho bạn ít hơn. Nó thực sự sẽ thu được nhiều hơn một chút từ cùng một lượt đặt phòng so với Hôm nay. Những gì nó đã làm là di chuyển khoản phí đến nơi mà bạn không thể nhìn thấy và nó đã công bố ngày chính xác mà nó dự định hoàn thành công việc. Đây là cách Airbnb kiếm tiền. Để theo dõi bất kỳ điều nào trong số đó, bạn phải biết số tiền hiện được chia như thế nào, đó là điều mà hầu hết mọi người đặt kỳ nghỉ chưa bao giờ có lý do để tập luyện. Hãy tưởng tượng mức giá hàng đêm mà số đêm đạt tới 1.000 đô la và 000 đô la đó là số máy chủ của bạn đã chọn. Airbnb sau đó tiến hành giao dịch hai lần. Máy chủ nào kết thúc với 970 sẽ được giảm 3% và thêm khoảng 14% cho bạn. Vậy là thẻ bị tính phí 1.140. Bạn đã thấy con số thứ hai đó. toàn bộ thời gian đặt trước của bạn nằm ở hàng riêng bên dưới tổng phụ. Và nó được cho là bị phàn nàn nhiều nhất về chi tiết đơn hàng trong du lịch hiện đại. $1,140 để lại trong tài khoản của bạn cho một ngôi nhà mà chủ sở hữu của nó nhận được 970 đô la. 170 còn lại thuộc về một công ty mà bạn sắp sở hữu không có gì ngủ nướng, không dọn dẹp gì và sẽ không đưa chìa khóa cho bạn. Vào ngày 7 tháng 7 năm nay, Airbnb đã xác nhận thời điểm thỏa thuận đó kết thúc. Các nước chủ nhà bên ngoài EU sẽ chuyển đi vào ngày 15 tháng 9. Tổ chức bên trong nó vào ngày 13 tháng 10 và từ đó có phí duy nhất 15 12% chủ nhà thanh toán đầy đủ. Dòng của bạn biến mất. Tôi sẽ không quyết định bạn nghĩ gì về điều đó vì bản thân khoản phí hóa ra là một nửa nhàm chán. Điều gì xảy ra với mức giá được quảng cáo sau đó mới là một nửa thú vị. Rất nhiều bạn đã tổ chức và tôi sẽ đến gặp bạn sau. Ai mới một lần làm khách thì để mình đặt cược nhé về bạn. Bạn chưa bao giờ kiểm tra những gì máy chủ của bạn thực sự nhận được. Bạn đã nhìn vào tổng số. Bạn đã gây ra một tiếng động nhỏ và vẫn đặt nó. Và sau đó bạn phàn nàn về khoản phí ở đâu đó giữa sân bay và phía trước cửa mà không bao giờ xác định được tiền đã đi đâu. Hãy tiếp tục và chứng minh tôi sai. Nếu bạn biết chủ nhà đã trả bao nhiêu cho lần đặt phòng trước, hãy đặt cả hai số liệu trong phần bình luận, số bạn đã trả và số họ nhận được. Và nếu bạn là chủ nhà, hãy đăng khoản thanh toán của bạn bên cạnh tổng số khách vì chủ nhà là những người duy nhất trong toàn bộ thỏa thuận này có thể nhìn thấy cả hai nửa tại once. Và khoảng trống sẽ làm điều gì đó để đoán mỗi khi ai đó đặt nó lên. Hãy thích video này nếu bạn từng tranh cãi với ai đó về phí Airbnb. Hãy đăng ký nếu bạn muốn biết tại sao nó tồn tại. Quay lại dòng biến mất, sau đó. Một máy chủ hiện đang thanh toán 970 đô la cho lượt đặt phòng trị giá 1.000 đô la đó sẽ bắt đầu vào tháng 9 tới một vấn đề vì Airbnb hiện có giá 15 USD. 5% của toàn bộ thay vì ba. Giữ nguyên danh sách và khoản thanh toán giảm xuống còn $845 cho cùng một ngôi nhà. Cùng một đêm và cùng một vị khách, giảm giá khoảng 13% cho không có lý do gì chủ nhà có thể giải thích cho mình. Không ai chấp nhận điều đó. Vì vậy, máy chủ sẽ làm điều duy nhất mà tình hình cho phép, đó là đẩy giá niêm yết tăng lên cho đến khi khoản thanh toán tăng trở lại mức cũ. Nhận được $970 ở phía bên kia của con số 15. Giảm 5% có nghĩa là quảng cáo địa điểm ở mức 1.148 USD. Hãy xem điều gì đã xảy ra với màn hình của bạn trong thời gian chờ đợi. Trước khi bạn nhìn chằm chằm vào một địa điểm trị giá 1.000 đô la với khoản phí 140 đô la được chốt vào nó, và sự khó chịu của bạn đã có mục tiêu. Sau đó, bạn đang tìm một nơi có giá 1.148 USD để ở mà không có phí ở bất cứ đâu trên trang và sự khó chịu không có gì đáng lo ngại. Bạn đang trả nhiều hơn $8 so với trước đây. Airbnb đang thu 178 thay vì 170. Máy chủ của bạn chính xác là nơi họ bắt đầu và là con số bị phẫn nộ nhất trong việc kinh doanh đã được xếp vào giá phòng nơi nó hiện nay đọc là thứ mà người dẫn chương trình đã quyết định thay vì thứ mà Airbnb đã lấy. Không ai giảm phí. Một khoản phí đã được chuyển thành một con số mà bạn đã đồng ý xem xét. Có một lý lẽ hợp lý ở phía bên kia của vấn đề này và nó xứng đáng nói chuẩn đấy. Khách thực sự thích một con số trung thực. Các khách sạn đã trải qua hai thập kỷ bị kiện về phí nghỉ dưỡng và định giá nhỏ giọt. Và các cơ quan quản lý ở một số quốc gia hiện nay yêu cầu phải trả trước tổng giá. Airbnb có thể đứng đó với vẻ mặt nghiêm túc và nói rằng cuối cùng nó cũng được trình chiếu cho bạn biết chi phí lưu trú là bao nhiêu và nó sẽ nói lên sự thật. Sự thật chỉ tình cờ đến vào đúng buổi sáng mà mọi người đã tức giận về việc trở nên không thể nhìn thấy. Quá nhiều cho phí. Quy mô của nó là một cú sốc riêng biệt. $91. 3 tỷ lượt đặt phòng đã được thực hiện thông qua Airbnb vào năm ngoái, đó là tổng số lượng khách được trả cho 533 triệu đêm và trải nghiệm. Ngoài dòng sông đó công ty giữ lại 12. 24 tỷ đồng, và con số đó là toàn bộ doanh thu của hãng. Mỗi đô la còn lại thuộc về ai đó có phòng ngủ trống hoặc căn hộ thứ hai, 13. 4%. Airbnb xử lý 91 tỷ USD giao dịch của người khác và giữ lại khoảng 1 USD trong mỗi giao dịch 7 rưỡi, nghe có vẻ gần như hạn chế cho đến khi bạn nhìn vào số tiền kiếm được nó có giá. Có hơn 8 triệu danh sách đang hoạt động trên nền tảng trải rộng trên nhiều hơn 220 quốc gia và Airbnb không sở hữu chính xác quốc gia nào trong số đó.
